title: Beckmann rearrangement
subtitle: An oxime in acid becomes an amide: cyclohexanone oxime to caprolactam

reactants.caption: cyclohexanone oxime + sulfuric acid
reactants.learnerPrompt: Make the oxime OH into a leaving group.
hintTiers: The N–O bond will break, and water is a much better leaving group than hydroxide. Where should the acid put its proton?
The OH oxygen takes the proton of sulfuric acid; the O–H pair stays on the acid's oxygen. Two arrows.
OH oxygen lone pair → new bond to the acidic proton of H₂SO₄; that O–H bond → a lone pair on the sulfuric acid oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The oxime nitrogen is in fact the most basic atom, but a proton there makes no leaving group. Protonate the OH: it leaves as water.
Hydroxide is a poor leaving group. Protonate the OH first.

protonated-oxime.caption: O-protonated oxime + hydrogensulfate
protonated-oxime.learnerPrompt: The key step: a carbon moves to nitrogen as water leaves.
hintTiers: Losing water from nitrogen on its own would leave a nitrogen with only six electrons. Which bond on the carbon of C=N can move onto nitrogen at the same time?
Three arrows: the N–O bond breaks onto oxygen, a ring C–C bond moves from the C=N carbon to nitrogen, and the nitrogen lone pair makes a C≡N bond.
N–O bond → a lone pair on oxygen (water leaves); ring C–C bond of the C=N carbon → new bond from that ring carbon to nitrogen; nitrogen lone pair → another C–N π bond.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: The ring carbon moves to the atom next door, nitrogen: a 1,2-shift. Oxygen leaves as water.
Water is the leaving group, so the N–O pair goes to oxygen.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Right that water leaves, but on its own that leaves nitrogen with six electrons. The ring C–C bond moves to nitrogen as water goes, and the nitrogen lone pair makes C≡N.

nitrilium-ion.caption: a cyclic nitrilium ion + water + hydrogensulfate
nitrilium-ion.learnerPrompt: Water adds to the nitrilium ion.
hintTiers: The nitrilium carbon is strongly electrophilic, like the carbon of a protonated nitrile. Which nucleophile is present?
The water oxygen bonds to the carbon of C≡N⁺, and one C≡N π pair moves onto nitrogen. Two arrows.
Water oxygen lone pair → new bond to the nitrilium carbon; one C–N π bond → a lone pair on nitrogen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Hydrogensulfate can add too, but that adduct only goes on to the same product with water. Draw water adding.
The π pair goes to nitrogen, the electronegative atom that carries the positive charge, not onto carbon.

imidate-oxonium.caption: water adduct (positive oxygen) + hydrogensulfate
imidate-oxonium.learnerPrompt: Remove a proton from the positive oxygen.
hintTiers: The oxygen that just bonded carries two hydrogens and a positive charge. Which base is present?
The hydrogensulfate oxygen takes one of the drawn protons; the O–H pair stays on oxygen. Two arrows.
Hydrogensulfate oxygen lone pair → new bond to a drawn H on the positive oxygen; that O–H bond → a lone pair on oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Water leaving takes you back to the nitrilium ion. Remove a proton instead.

imidic-acid.caption: the imidic acid (lactim) + sulfuric acid
hintTiers: An imidic acid is the less stable tautomer of an amide, as an enol is of a ketone. The hydrogen on oxygen must end up on nitrogen. In acid, which happens first: add a proton or take one away?
The nitrogen lone pair takes the proton of sulfuric acid; the O–H pair stays on the acid's oxygen. Two arrows.
Nitrogen lone pair → new bond to the acidic proton of H₂SO₄; that O–H bond → a lone pair on the sulfuric acid oxygen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Protonating the OH just goes back a step. Protonate the nitrogen: the proton has to end up there.

protonated-imidic-acid.caption: N-protonated imidic acid + hydrogensulfate
protonated-imidic-acid.learnerPrompt: Tautomerism, part 2: remove the O–H proton and form the C=O.
hintTiers: Losing the O–H proton should let oxygen form a C=O. Where do the C=N π electrons go?
Hydrogensulfate takes the O–H proton; the O–H pair becomes a C=O π bond, and the C=N π pair moves onto nitrogen. Three arrows.
Hydrogensulfate oxygen lone pair → new bond to the O–H hydrogen; O–H bond → C=O π bond; C=N π bond → a lone pair on nitrogen.

misconceptions.feedbackMessage: Taking the proton back off nitrogen just undoes the last step. Remove the O–H proton.

partialProgressMessages.feedbackMessage: Good: the C=O bond forms. Now the carbon has five bonds: move the C=N π pair onto nitrogen.

steps.explanationAfterStep: The OH becomes OH₂⁺: water is a good leaving group from nitrogen.

The ring carbon anti-periplanar to the leaving water moves to nitrogen as the N–O bond breaks: the group trans to the OH migrates. (The app does not check that geometry yet; in cyclohexanone oxime both ring carbons are the same.) The nitrogen joins the ring, which grows from six to seven atoms, and the nitrogen lone pair makes a nitrilium ion.
Water adds to the nitrilium carbon.
Losing a proton gives the imidic acid, the tautomer of an amide with C=N–OH in place of N–C=O.
The proton goes onto nitrogen. The cation is shared with oxygen: it is also a protonated amide.
Losing the O–H proton gives caprolactam, the cyclic amide that is polymerised to nylon 6. Overall the oxime has become an amide, and the ring has gained a nitrogen.

mechanismSummary: Protonation turns the oxime OH into a leaving group. As water leaves, the ring carbon anti to it moves from carbon to nitrogen, and the nitrogen lone pair makes a nitrilium ion. Water adds to the nitrilium carbon, and proton transfers turn the imidic acid into its more stable tautomer, the amide: caprolactam, the monomer of nylon 6.
references: Clayden, Greeves and Warren, Organic Chemistry, 2nd edition (Oxford University Press), chapter 36
